title: The canonical register: Hēlios

body:
# The canonical register: Hēlios

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Hēlios, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Hēlios to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The name is attested as **Ἥλιος**, as LSJ and Beekes record. On the evidence, it means "Sun (from PIE *seh₂wel-)". The canonical transliteration is **Hēlios**.

And the marks themselves: **e → ē** (Eta: long epsilon). Remove any one of them and you have not simplified the name — you have told a small lie about it, and small lies in references have long consequences.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'HAY-lee-oss' — the first syllable rises like the sun; the rest is bright and clear. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *helios* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *helios* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible. Every mark it drops — *e → ē* — is a fact the sources recorded. A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

Now to the forms that provoked your letter. As for *Helīos*: it comes from macron roulette — pages that know a long vowel exists somewhere in the name and plant the bar on the wrong one, and it fails because lengthens i when the attested long vowel is e (Eta: long epsilon); moving the bar is not a small error — it asserts a different Greek word

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The Romans identified Hēlios with Sol, though Apollo increasingly absorbed solar attributes in both Greek and Roman religion.  The emperor Aurelian made Sol Invictus the official patron of the Roman Empire in 274 CE, and the cult influenced the dating of Christmas.

And it never stopped working. Hēlios is the namesake of heliocentrism, helium, and countless words for sunlight.  The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was a giant statue of Hēlios.

## The Convention's Own History

The marks this register defends were not invented for typesetting. Ancient Greek carried a melodic pitch accent, and the acute and circumflex were added by Alexandrian scholars — Aristophanes of Byzantium, tradition holds — precisely to preserve it when the spoken language began to level. Vowel quantity (the macron's concern) is older still: it changes meter, meaning, and grammar, and the poets of the Theogony depend on it. To drop either class of mark is to drop two millennia of deliberate preservation. The restored-stress convention simply continues the oldest documented project in European scholarship: keeping the sound of Greek alive in its letters.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Hēlios** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *helios* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Hēlios** stands at [/sites/helios/](/sites/helios/).
